extracted.intended_audience: General readers, students, writers, educators, facilitators, and researchers interested in dialogue (literary, philosophical, pedagogical, and practical facilitation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for using dialogue as a literary form, philosophical device, pedagogical method, and facilitated practice; covers types (Socratic, Bohm, structured, egalitarian), their aims, and characteristic features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: An interactive communication between two or more people, and a literary and theatrical form that depicts such an exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general standard, dialogue denotes conversational exchange; it is used across literature, theatre, philosophy, pedagogy, and facilitation. Recognize that the term also has historical and linguistic roots (Greek diálogos — 'through' + logos — 'speech, reason').

rubrics_metrics.name: Socratic/Platonic dialogue (philosophical dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A form simplified by Plato into 'pure argumentative conversation' focusing on dialectic examination of philosophical questions, often featuring Socrates as speaker and interlocutors discussing some philosophical question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating a Platonic/Socratic dialogue, expect concentrated argumentation and philosophical probing rather than narrative ornamentation; the form can be used to advance systematic reasoning and expose assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary dialogue: balance of argument and character-drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical antecedents (mimes) combined amusing character-drawing with conversational action; Plato reduced it toward argument, while later literary dialogues alternate between character depiction and argumentative content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In literary use, consider whether the dialogue aims primarily at characterisation, anecdote/wit, or philosophical argument — strong literary dialogue typically balances realistic speech and characterization with purpose (plot, theme, idea). Avoid rendering dialogue purely as information-dump without character or dramatic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bohm dialogue principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A form where participants (typically 10–30) agree to leave behind debate tactics and instead talk from their own experience about improvised subjects to explore assumptions of thinking, meaning, communication, and social effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitation should discourage persuasion tactics and encourage speaking from personal experience. The aim is collective inquiry into assumptions rather than winning arguments. Use regular meetings of a few hours or multi-day sessions for depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bakhtinian dialogic relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogic relations are specific and cannot be reduced to purely logical or purely linguistic phenomena; they occur between complete utterances of speaking subjects and presuppose language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses or designs of dialogue should treat utterances as whole, socially-situated acts; dialogue is not merely exchange of propositions but intersubjective interplay between voices. Avoid treating dialogues as only logical structures detached from social voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egalitarian dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: A dialogue in which contributions are considered according to the validity of their reasoning, instead of according to the status or power of those who make them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dialogic learning and classroom use, design conditions that foreground argument validity and equal respect rather than hierarchical authority. Ensure mechanisms that let less-powerful participants contribute and be evaluated on reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured dialogue (facilitated/problem-oriented)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplined form where participants follow a dialogue framework or a facilitator to orient discourse toward problem understanding and consensual action, particularly useful when unstructured dialogue is insufficient for coordinating multiple perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frameworks and facilitators to ensure adequate stakeholder representation, balanced contributions, and progress toward shared understanding or action. Structured dialogue is appropriate for complex problems like peacemaking, indigenous community development, policy formulation, and youth engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for structuring dialogues (representation and balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured dialogue is used to ensure a sufficient variety of stakeholders represents the problem system of concern, and that voices and contributions are equally balanced in the dialogic process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When convening dialogues for public policy or community issues, proactively include diverse stakeholders, set ground rules or facilitation to prevent domination, and aim for balanced participation. Distinguish structured dialogue from ordinary discussion or deliberation when coordination and representation are primary goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogical pedagogy (Freirean principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogued communication allows students and teachers to learn from one another in an environment characterised by respect and equality; dialogued pedagogy links learning to praxis—action informed by people's values—to make positive social change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational dialogue should be mutual (not top-down), promote respect and equality, connect reflection with action, and be attentive to oppressed or marginalized voices. Evaluate pedagogical dialogue by its capacity to foster learning and social praxis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral dialogues: components and closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral dialogues involve establishing a moral baseline; sociological 'dialogue starters'; linking multiple groups' discussions ('megalogues'); distinguishing the moral-dialogue attributes from rational deliberations or culture wars; dramatization to attract attention; and closure through establishing a new shared moral understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using dialogue to shift communal moral views, plan for stages (baseline, starters, linkage, dramatization, closure) and measure success by whether a new shared moral understanding is established. Avoid conflating moral dialogue with mere debate—aim for processes that enable genuine communal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogical leadership (acting dialogically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue as a form of thinking, acting and speaking where 'acting dialogically' means directing someone's attention to another person and to reality simultaneously; dialogical leadership embeds dialogue in organizational management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders using dialogical approaches should practice attention to others and reality, foster participative communication, and replace purely hierarchical HR practices with dialogic processes. Evaluate leadership by its ability to cultivate mutual understanding and collective sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical uses and settings for dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is used in a variety of settings—from education to business—and as a practice for problem understanding and consensual action; variants include classroom dialogue, Bohm dialogue, structured dialogue, and facilitation for couples or community development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the dialogue form to match context: use egalitarian classroom dialogue for learning, Bohm dialogue for exploring assumptions, structured dialogue for complex stakeholder problems, and tailored dialogue methods (e.g., couples' dialogue techniques) for relational work. Consider group size, facilitator role, and desired outcome when choosing form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminological sensitivity (colloquium vs dialogus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations and uses of 'dialogue' may conflate Latin terms with distinct meanings (e.g., colloquium 'discussion' vs dialogus 'dialogue'), and word choice can reflect conceptual differences influenced by thinkers like Buber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of subtle distinctions in terminology when analyzing historical texts or institutional documents; choice of word may signal different expectations (discussion, debate, dialogue) and affect how a practice should be organized or evaluated.
